title: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention
text: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention Protecting the health of Nigerians Archive Months Weeks Recent Publication Advanced NFETP FAQ Saturday, April 10, 2021 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is Advanced NFETP? To address the different levels of expertise required at the national, state and local government levels, the NFETP is being implemented as a three-tiered pyramidal model: the Integrated Training for Surveillance Officers in Nigeria (ITSON), the Intermediate NFETP (I-NFETP) and the Advanced NFETP (A-NFETP) The Advanced Nigeria Field Epidemiology Training Programme (NFETP) is a two-year in-service training programme which provides competency-based training and service delivery in applied epidemiology and public health. It is coordinated by the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH), Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (FMARD) and Federal Ministry of Environment (FMEnv). The programme aims to build workforce capacity in disease surveillance and response, with dedicated mentorship using the One Health approach. The trainees support and contribute to the growth of public health capacity at national and state levels during the training and gain practical experience through field placements. Is the NFETP an accredited programme? Yes. The NFETP was accredited by the Global Accreditation Body of Training Programs in Epidemiology and Public Health Interventions Network (TEPHINET) in 2018. How does NFETP help the country? • Residents and graduates of the NFETP are trained with skills required to prevent, prepare for, rapidly detect and respond to disease outbreaks and public health threats. • They enhance the country’s public health workforce, contributing to national and global health security. What impact has the NFETP had on the country? NFETP residents and graduates have responded to a range of outbreaks both within the country and internationally. The outbreaks responded to include communicable diseases such as viral haemorrhagic fevers, meningitis, cholera and COVID-19 as well as environmental hazards such as lead poisoning. What are the programme objectives? To train future leaders in applied epidemiology using a solutions-based approach to public health events. To provide epidemiological capacity as part of Nigeria?s health security To strengthen public health surveillance systems for human, animal, and environmental health. To strengthen the One Health approach to outbreak preparedness and response, including the linkage between public health, veterinary public health, and environmental health. To develop capacity that will contribute effectively to public health research activities for human, animal and environmental health. To improve communications and networking among public health practitioners and researchers in Nigeria and across African countries. To strengthen affiliations with international organisations, such as the Training Programmes in Epidemiology and Public Health Interventions Network (TEPHINET), AFENET and other applied epidemiology and laboratory training programmes. What is the plan of work and timeline for NFETP? • It is a full-time two-year in-service training programme in field epidemiology that provides competency based training and service delivery in applied epidemiology and public health. • It is 70% field based and 30% classroom based. Is there any oversight committee for the programme? Yes. The Advisory Board which is chaired by the Honourable Minister of Health will provide oversight for the programme to ensure it meets its objectives. The Implementation Committee chaired by the Director General of NCDC will provide oversight for day-to-day operations of the programme Where is the management of the programme located? The NCDC as the National Public Health Institute (NPHI) in Nigeria has the mandate as contained in the NCDC Act, to lead the coordination of the NFETP with support from partners. What skills will be expected from the graduate? It is expected that an NFETP graduate will acquire the following skills: Epidemiological Methods Biostatistics Public Health Surveillance Laboratory and Biostatistics Communication Computer Technology Management and Leadership Prevention effectiveness Teaching and Mentoring Epidemiology of priority diseases and injuries What certification will the graduates of the NFETP receive? Graduates will be given a final certificate signed by the NCDC DG. How will the training be conducted? • Training is largely practical and field-based. • It is divided into 70% field work and 30% class work (didactic component), with the latter conducted in Abuja. What is the maximum number of candidates the NFETP recruit? The number of candidates is limited to some factors including the availability of funding, priority field placements, space for training, size of the recruiting pool and availability of career opportunities. What are the career opportunities for graduates of NFETP? These include: • Locally: - Epidemiologist (e.g., in national disease prevention and control programmes or State Ministry of Health) - Programme Manager (e.g., in national disease control programmes) • Internationally: - Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) with public health functions How is the NFETP funded? The programme is currently funded by the Government of Nigeria, with support from the World Bank through the Regional Disease Surveillance Systems Enhancement (REDISSE) project. It is also supported by partners. Do I need to pay for the programme? The programme is currently fully funded, and residents will be provided with stipends to support them while on the programme. Can I work during the programme? The programme is full-time, so, a letter of release from your or workplace is required. Who is qualified/eligible to apply? To apply for this fellowship, you must have: A Master of Public Health (MPH) degree or Masters? degree (MSc) in epidemiology, statistics,

title: Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties Why exiting Nigeria does not end a company’s tax duties Ademide Flower-Olumide September 15, 2026 Share ads Corporate exits do not erase tax obligations Companies may close offices, sell assets, end operations, and even move elsewhere, but exiting Nigeria does not automatically end their tax affairs. Under Nigeria’s new tax administration framework, businesses that cease operations still must file outstanding and final tax returns, raising questions about how tax authorities handle companies after they exit the market. This issue has gained renewed relevance following Uber’s restructuring in Nigeria, highlighting a broader question for multinational companies: what happens to their tax affairs when they leave? Tax expert Nojeem Yusuf explained that a business leaving a country does not conclude its obligations immediately. Companies still need to submit final tax returns, as cessation does not stop outstanding tax liabilities, ongoing disputes, or the authority’s ability to examine corporate affairs. According to the Nigeria Tax Administration Act (NTAA) 2025, any company that permanently ceases trade or business in Nigeria must file tax returns for the cessation year alongside any outstanding returns. Read also: Six months into Nigeria’s tax reforms, businesses demand certainty The law requires companies to file these returns within six months of permanently ceasing operations in Nigeria. Furthermore, if revenue authorities have initiated audits, corporations must remain engaged to resolve those audits and settle any additional tax due. Even without ongoing audits, an exit triggers tax authorities to commence examinations. Managing winding up and related party transactions Shutting down operations is not the final step in a company’s relationship with tax authorities. The NTAA requires every company to designate a representative to manage its tax affairs, running concurrently with the corporate winding-up process governed by the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020. Writing on the implications of the new law, tax specialist Chizoba Ngwudo noted that insolvency or winding up does not absolve a business of its tax responsibilities. Outstanding liabilities remain collectible from remaining assets and, under specific circumstances, responsible officers. ads ads The tax question becomes more complex when the entity leaving Nigeria is a subsidiary of a multinational group whose parent company continues operations abroad. Although the Nigerian company ceases local operations, transactions between the subsidiary and its foreign parent or related entities remain relevant to the tax authority. This scrutiny is vital when handling outstanding intercompany balances or transferring assets during an exit. Nigeria’s tax framework requires connected transactions to comply with the arm’s length principle, ensuring terms reflect independent market conditions. Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Read also: Nigeria’s informal economy is more than tax evasion, expert says Tax advisers emphasise that corporate closures and physical shutdowns are separate procedures. Multinationals must distinguish between restructuring, transferring a business to another entity, or formally winding up and dissolving the local company. PwC Nigeria highlights voluntary winding up, deregistration, and striking a company’s name from the Register of Companies as distinct routes for managing exit affairs. Protecting the national revenue base The scale of company income tax collected by the government underscores why departing businesses matter to Nigeria’s revenue base. According to National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) data, Nigeria collected N9.21 trillion in Company Income Tax (CIT) in 2025, representing a 41 percent increase from the previous year. In the first quarter of 2026, CIT collections stood at N1.37 trillion, demonstrating that corporate taxpayers continue to account for a significant pool of government revenue. Foreign CIT payments formed a substantial portion of these collections, reflecting the vital contribution of multinational and non-domestic businesses. ads ads Read also: MAN seeks forex backlog payout, 2025 tax law clarity To ensure full compliance before departure, tax experts recommend a structured action plan: Identify outstanding tax returns and file cessation returns within the six-month statutory period. Reconcile tax records with the revenue authority and properly challenge disputed liabilities within applicable timelines. Review related-party transactions, transfer-pricing documentation, and the treatment of disposed assets as part of the exit strategy. title: Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps Businesses seek joint tax audits as federal, state authorities face coordination gaps Ademide Flower-Olumide September 16, 2026 Share ads Businesses are seeking better coordination between federal and state authorities, including joint audits, as stakeholders say overlapping tax engagements remain one of the weak areas in the implementation of Nigeria’s new tax regime. Emeka Chime, tax partner at PwC, said businesses want the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) and state authorities to work together more closely to reduce repeated audits and compliance issues. “The law provides a framework for joint audits, and so that is something that tax payers have to see being implemented”, Chime said at the 2026 LCCI-OPS Stakeholders’ Forum on Emerging Tax Matters in Lagos. He emphasised that businesses currently face situations where they may undergo an audit by the NRS and subsequently receive another audit by the Lagos State Internal Revenue Service (LIRS), thereby creating additional compliance demands. This was noted as businesses adjust to the tax reforms that took effect in 2026, with stakeholders at the forum stating that implementation will depend not only on the legislation but also on how easily businesses can comply. ads ads The Executive Chairman of LIRS, represented by Mustafa Foluso, the director of tax audit, said tax reform will succeed better if taxpayers understood the changes, ensures compliance and have confidence in how the system was administered. “Compliance should be made easier, less costly for those willing to comply, while deliberate non compliance should become easier to identify,” he said. He added that technology and data would better shape tax administration by helping authorities understand taxpayers’ behaviour, identify compliance risks and provide more targeted services. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 The LIRS representative also identified simplification, engagement and collaboration as top key priorities for the next phase of implementation. ads ads Meanwhile, Richard Ayibiowu, president and chairman of the Nigeria Employers’ Consultative Association (NECA), said taxpayers were now embracing their obligations more but still expected clearer benefits from paying taxes. He reflected on the popular Lagos slogan “ Sanwo Ori e, Jaiye lo ” meaning “Pay your tax, enjoy yourself” emphasising that taxpayers were still looking for more in terms of enjoying the benefits of taxation. He said taxpayers were still looking for actual evidence that their tax payments were translating into development and tangible benefits. The Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria similarly urged continued engagement between government, tax authorities and the private sector, alongside greater use of technology and data to reduce duplication and unnecessary physical interaction. The institute said tax reform should not be judged solely by higher revenue but also by whether it improves compliance, broadens the tax base, and strengthen taxpayer confidence. The forum therefore highlighted an early test for Nigeria’s tax reforms: whether increased revenue and compliance can be matched by a tax system that is clearer, more coordinated, and easier for taxpayers to navigate. Ademide Flower-Olumide Ayomide Odunlami is a Tax Reporter at BusinessDay, covering Nigeria’s tax reforms, compliance trends, and government revenue strategies. She reports on how evolving tax policies affect businesses, investors, and the broader economy, providing clarity on complex regulatory issues through data-driven journalism. title: FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears FirstHoldCo crosses N7trn market cap as FTSE Frontier 50 debut nears Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads FirstHoldCo Plc, the parent company of FirstBank, crossed the N7 trillion market capitalisation mark on Friday, as its shares rallied ahead of the group’s entry into the FTSE Frontier 50 Index. The financial services group’s shares rose 8.1 percent to N160 from N148, lifting its market value to about N7.28 trillion, based on data from the Nigerian Exchange Limited. The milestone sustains FirstHoldCo lead as the most valuable listed Nigerian bank by market capitalisation, ahead of Zenith Bank and Guaranty Trust Holding Company (GTCO). The rally came on the final trading session before FirstHoldCo’s inclusion in the FTSE Frontier 50 Index, with the revised index taking effect from Monday, September 21. FTSE Russell included FirstHoldCo alongside five other Nigerian companies — Zenith Bank, GTCO, MTN Nigeria, Dangote Cement and Aradel Holdings — in its latest review of the 50-stock frontier-market benchmark. The changes take effect after the close of trading on Friday. ads ads The inclusion coincides with Nigeria’s return to FTSE Russell’s Frontier Market classification, ending a three-year period in which the country was designated Unclassified. FTSE catalyst For FirstHoldCo, the FTSE Frontier 50 inclusion gives the bank greater visibility among global investors and puts its shares within a concentrated benchmark covering 50 companies across frontier markets. The index comprises the largest companies in the broader FTSE Frontier Index universe, subject to requirements including market capitalisation, liquidity, free float and investability. ads ads The timing is significant because the Friday session was the last opportunity for investors to adjust positions before the new index composition becomes effective. Read also: Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone While inclusion does not automatically translate into a specific amount of foreign capital, it can increase demand from investors whose portfolios track or benchmark against the index. FirstHoldCo’s chairman, Femi Otedola, described the inclusion as a “defining milestone” for the group, saying it reflected the transformation of the financial services company and investor confidence in the institution. Otedola’s expanding bet The latest market-cap milestone also adds to the sharp increase in the value of Otedola’s stake in FirstHoldCo. Otedola has spent about N351.2 billion increasing his stake in the financial services group through five disclosed purchases since July 22, according to the transactions disclosed to the market. Related News IGP vows thorough probe into deaths of 37 suspected miners Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment His latest disclosed acquisition, made through his investment vehicle Calvados Global Services Limited, involved the purchase of 95.7 million FirstHoldCo shares for N12.58 billion on August 24. The purchase took his total holding to about 12.23 billion shares, representing approximately 26.6 percent of FirstHoldCo based on the figures in the company’s disclosures. The chairman’s accumulation has coincided with a sharp appreciation in the bank’s share price, helping to push the group’s market value beyond the N7 trillion threshold. Earnings underpin rally The share-price gains have also come against a backdrop of stronger operating performance. FirstHoldCo reported N526.13 billion in profit after tax for the first half of 2026, while its cost-to-income ratio improved to 44.2 percent. The group has also received shareholder approval for a N253.1 billion capital-raising programme, part of efforts to strengthen its balance sheet and support its growth ambitions. The combination of earnings, capital-raising plans, sustained investor interest and the forthcoming FTSE inclusion has helped reshape the market’s perception of FirstHoldCo. The bank’s valuation milestone is particularly notable given the scale of the recent rally in its shares, which has pushed the company from a market capitalisation of N5 trillion in late July to more than N7 trillion. From N5trn to N7trn FirstHoldCo crossed the N5 trillion market-capitalisation threshold in late July, following Otedola’s increased stake in the group. The latest move means the bank has added more than N2 trillion in market value in a relatively short period, highlighting the extent of the repricing of the stock. The FTSE Frontier 50 inclusion now provides another potential catalyst as FirstHoldCo enters a benchmark followed by international investors. For Nigeria’s capital market, the development also comes at a significant moment. The country’s return to FTSE Russell’s Frontier Market classification restores Nigerian equities to the index provider’s global frontier-market framework after three years of being Unclassified. FTSE Russell said its assessment found no material settlement, operational or funding issues following Nigeria’s transition from T+2 to T+1 settlement. FirstHoldCo’s rise above N7 trillion therefore reflects more than a single day’s share-price gain. It places the bank at the intersection of stronger earnings, increased shareholder accumulation, a major capital-raising programme and renewed international market visibility as Nigeria returns to the global frontier-market universe. title: How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Economy > How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments How investors can legally reduce tax they pay on investments Ayomide Odunlami August 31, 2026 Share ads Nigerians investing in shares, bonds, funds, property, and other assets can legally reduce the tax they pay by taking advantage of exemptions and favourable tax treatments under the country’s new tax regime. The Nigeria Tax Act 2025, which took effect on January 1, 2026, changed the treatment of several forms of investment income and gains, making tax an increasingly important consideration for investors when assessing returns. LessaTax, in an article titled “How Nigerians Can Legally Reduce the Tax They Pay on Their Investments,” highlights several ways investors can structure their investments to take advantage of exemptions and reduce their tax burden while remaining compliant with the law. Read also: How Nigeria is using tax breaks to lure oil investors Government bonds can offer tax-free income ads ads One of the clearest opportunities is in government securities. Income from federal and state government bonds is exempt from tax under the new law, according to an article by Udo Udoma & Belo-Osagie titled ‘Key Tax Incentives Under the Nigeria Tax Act.’ This means investors comparing two investments with similar headline returns may end up with different after-tax amounts depending on the security chosen. For instance, a lower-yielding government bond could deliver a more competitive return after tax than a higher-yielding taxable investment because the bond income is exempt. ads ads The tax treatment should not, however, be the only consideration, as risk, liquidity, and expected return also determine the attractiveness of an investment. Collective investment schemes can also offer tax advantages Investors can also reduce their tax exposure by considering how they invest, not just what they invest in. Collective investment schemes pool money from investors and invest in assets such as shares and bonds. Dividends distributed by authorised collective investment schemes are exempt from income tax under the Nigeria Tax Act. Udo Udoma & Belo-Osagie said the exemption could make collective investment schemes more attractive to retail investors by reducing the tax disadvantage associated with investing through such vehicles. This means investors should consider not only what an investment earns, but also how the income is distributed and taxed. Read also: MAN seeks safeguards for manufacturers under new tax law Foreign investment income comes with conditions Investors earning income from abroad may also benefit from specific exemptions, although these come with conditions. Certain foreign-sourced dividends, interest, rent, and royalties can qualify for exemption where they are brought into Nigeria in convertible currency through approved channels and paid into an approved local bank account, according to PwC. Simply investing abroad, however, does not automatically make the income tax-free. Investors need to meet the conditions attached to the exemption and understand their wider Nigerian tax obligations. Under the new regime, individuals no longer pay the former flat 10 percent capital gains tax on chargeable gains. PwC said capital gains for individuals are now taxed at the applicable progressive personal income tax rates. The law nevertheless provides relief for some share disposals. Gains from the disposal of shares can qualify for exemption where the proceeds do not exceed N150 million in any 12 consecutive months, and the attributable gain does not exceed N10 million, according to PwC. Certain proceeds reinvested in shares can also qualify for relief. This makes it important for investors to understand the tax consequences before selling a large portfolio rather than after the transaction has been completed. No withholding tax does not always mean no tax Investors should also distinguish between withholding tax and their final tax liability. The absence of withholding tax on a particular investment income does not automatically mean the income is tax-free. Likewise, tax deducted at source may in some circumstances serve as a credit against the investor’s final liability rather than being the final tax. Understanding the distinction can prevent investors from underestimating what they may eventually owe. Tax planning starts before the investment For investors, tax planning should begin when they are deciding where to put their money, not when the tax bill arrives. A 17 percent return on a taxable investment, for example, cannot be assessed in isolation from a 15 percent return that is exempt from tax. The investor needs to compare what each option actually leaves in their pocket after tax, while also considering the risks involved. The same applies to someone deciding whether to invest directly in securities or through an authorised fund, or an investor holding foreign assets who needs to determine whether the conditions for an exemption have been met. Nigeria’s new tax regime therefore makes after-tax return a more important part of investment decisions. text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Seplat shares surge 166% as stock nears N15,000 milestone Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads … Elumelu’s stake gains about N311bn Seplat Energy Plc’s shares have surged 165.9 percent year-to-date to a record N14,907.80, making the oil and gas producer one of the strongest-performing large stocks on the Nigerian market as investors respond to stronger earnings and increased production. The stock gained 10 percent on September 10, rising from N13,552.60 to N14,907.80, according to Nigerian Exchange data, and remained at the record level through September 16. At N14,907.80, Seplat has gained 165.9 percent from N5,610 at the start of 2026 and is up 177.1 percent from N5,379 a year ago. The scale of the rally means investors who held the stock at the beginning of the year have seen the value of their investment more than double, underscoring the strength of the recent re-rating of the company. ads ads The rally has also been mirrored in Seplat’s London listing, where the shares, traded under the ticker SEPL, reached an all-time high of 845 pence on September 16 before closing at 839p. Read also: Seplat crosses N8trn valuation, stock hits 52-week high The London-listed stock subsequently fell 2.7 percent to 816p on September 17, but remained substantially above its 768p level on September 10. Strong earnings provide fundamental support ads ads The sharp appreciation in Seplat’s stock has come alongside a significant improvement in its financial performance. For the six months ended June 2026, the company’s profit before tax increased 74.1 percent year-on-year to N790.4 billion, from N454.1 billion in the corresponding period of last year. Revenue rose 15.5 percent to N2.50 trillion, while production increased to 139,509 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The earnings performance has strengthened the fundamental case for the stock, particularly as Seplat continues to benefit from its expanded production base following the consolidation of its offshore assets. In 2025, the company recorded average group production of 131,506 boepd, while annual revenue reached a record $2.73 billion. The increase in production is important for investors because higher output gives Seplat greater exposure to crude oil prices and provides additional scope for revenue and cash-flow growth. However, the magnitude of the stock’s appreciation has significantly exceeded the growth in revenue and profit, suggesting that market expectations about the company’s future performance are also playing a role in the re-rating. London rally reinforces investor demand Seplat’s performance in London provides another indication of the strength of investor interest in the company. Unlike the Nigerian listing, where the stock has remained at N14,907.80 since September 10, the London-listed shares continued to move higher over subsequent trading sessions. The shares rose from 768p on September 10 to 777p on September 11, 796p on September 14, 822p on September 15 and 839p on September 16, when they briefly touched 845p. Read also: Tony Elumelu’s Seplat stake rises to $1.28 billion as shares gain 8.4% The simultaneous appreciation in both markets suggests that the rally is not simply a function of trading conditions on the Nigerian market. It also gives investors a broader view of how Seplat is being valued internationally, particularly as the company expands its production base and strengthens its position as one of Africa’s significant independent energy producers. Oil prices and geopolitical risks add to the backdrop Global oil-market volatility has provided another important backdrop to the performance of energy stocks. Heightened tensions involving the United States and Iran, alongside uncertainty over vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, have increased volatility in global energy markets. For oil producers, higher crude prices can improve revenue and cash-flow expectations, although the effect depends on realised prices, production levels, costs, hedging and other factors. Seplat’s stock performance should therefore not be attributed to oil prices alone. The company’s stronger production, earnings growth and expanded asset base provide company-specific drivers, while movements in global crude markets influence the broader valuation environment for energy producers. Read also: Nigerian tycoon Tony Elumelu set to earn another $14.45m from Seplat Energy dividend Elumelu’s stake gains about N311bn The rally has also significantly increased the value of major shareholder holdings. Tony Elumelu’s indirect 120.4 million-share stake, held through Heirs Energies and Heirs Holdings, was worth about N1.48 trillion when Seplat traded at N12,320.60 on September 1. At the current record price of N14,907.80, the holding is worth approximately N1.79 trillion. That represents an increase of about N311.5 billion in the value of the stake in just over two weeks. The increase illustrates the wealth effect of Seplat’s rally for its major shareholders and shows how quickly changes in the stock price can translate into large movements in the value of strategic holdings. title: Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief Sterling Holdings reshuffles board, appoints former Ecobank risk chief Muhammed Lawal September 18, 2026 Share ads Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc has appointed Laoye Jaiyeola and Chinedu Ikwudinma as independent non-executive directors of Sterling Bank Limited, following the retirement of three directors at the expiration of their tenure. The Nigerian banking group also announced the retirement of Tunde Adeola, an executive director of Sterling Bank, after he attained the prescribed retirement age. The changes were disclosed in a statement on Wednesday signed by Sunny Kanabe, company secretary of the group. The retiring directors are Michael Ajukwu, Olusola Oworu and Olaitan Kajero, who left the board following the expiration of their respective tenures. The board expressed its appreciation to the retiring directors “for their dedication, leadership and contributions to the growth of the group” and wished them success in their future endeavours. ads ads Jaiyeola brings 35 years of financial services experience Jaiyeola joins the board with more than 35 years of experience spanning financial services, corporate governance and public policy in Nigeria. He spent nearly two decades at the Central Bank of Nigeria and later served as managing director and CEO of Kakawa Discount House Limited, now Quest Merchant Bank. He has held several senior leadership and board positions, including president of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria and chief executive officer of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group. ads ads Jaiyeola currently serves on the board of FMDQ Group Plc, the NESG Advisory Board and the Policy Innovation Centre. He holds a B.Sc. in Economics from Obafemi Awolowo University, a master’s degree in Banking and Finance from the University of Lagos and an MBA from Bangor University. He is a Fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria and the Chartered Institute of Directors. He is also a Chartered Member of the Chartered Banker Institute, Scotland. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 Jaiyeola is a Senior Executive Fellow of Harvard Kennedy School and founder and pro-chancellor of Hillside University of Science and Technology. Ikwudinma brings Ecobank, Citibank experience Ikwudinma was appointed an independent non-executive director of Sterling Bank effective August 20, 2026. He brings more than three decades of international banking and financial services experience, spanning risk management, corporate and investment banking, commercial banking, transaction banking, strategic leadership and governance across African and global markets. He spent more than two decades with Citibank, holding senior leadership positions in Nigeria, Zambia and Uganda. Ikwudinma served as managing director and chief executive officer of Citibank Uganda and as executive director and country risk manager for Citibank Nigeria. He most recently served as group chief risk officer of Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, having previously served as the group’s chief credit officer. Before joining Ecobank, he was the pioneer managing director of Nova Merchant Bank Limited. He currently serves as chairman of CS&C Associates Limited. Ikwudinma holds a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Civil Engineering from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, an M.Sc. in Structural Engineering and an MBA in Finance from the University of Lagos. He is a Fellow of the Nigerian Institute of Credit Administration and a Member of the Institute of Directors. The appointments strengthen Sterling Bank’s board with additional expertise in risk management, credit, financial services, corporate governance and international banking as the lender continues to execute its growth strategy. title: How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Africa > How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook How Nigerian, South African lenders are rewriting Africa’s banking M&A playbook Bunmi Bailey September 18, 2026 Share ads Nigerian and South African banks are taking increasingly different approaches to expansion across Africa, with Nigerian lenders favouring a series of acquisitions while South African groups are placing fewer but significantly larger controlling bets, a new report shows. The divergence is emerging as cross-border banking mergers and acquisitions accelerate across East Africa, with Kenya attracting the greatest deal value and Tanzania developing as a secondary market for banks seeking to build regional platforms. The M&A Trends in East Africa Banking Sector report by Deals & Advisory Report tracks six major banking transactions between 2024 and mid-2026 and identifies four acquiring banking groups. Nigerian and South African banks are the dominant acquirers, with most transactions targeting between 66 percent and 100 percent ownership, giving buyers control over operations and greater freedom to integrate businesses. “Almost every deal targets 66 to 100 percent ownership — buyers want operational control and integration freedom,” the report said. ads ads “Kenya is the clear centre of gravity, with Tanzania as a secondary platform-building market. Nigerian banks, led by Access Bank and followed by Zenith, have pursued volume through sequential deals, while South Africa’s Nedbank placed one large controlling bet on NCBA Group, the region’s flagship transaction at roughly $856 million.” Read also: Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit The contrasting strategies point to a broader shift in African banking M&A: banks are increasingly buying capabilities, licences, customer relationships and distribution networks rather than simply adding assets to their balance sheets. Nigeria’s volume strategy Access Bank has emerged as the most active Nigerian acquirer in the region, according to the report. ads ads Its transactions include the acquisition of National Bank of Kenya, BancABC Tanzania and Standard Chartered’s consumer, private and business banking business in Tanzania. The National Bank of Kenya transaction was valued at about KSh15.8 billion, or roughly $100 million-$110 million, while in Tanzania, Access used BancABC as a platform before adding Standard Chartered’s banking relationships and capabilities. Zenith Bank has followed a similar strategy, including its acquisition of Paramount Bank in Tanzania for more than $7.7 million. The strategy allows Nigerian banks to build regional footprints through multiple transactions, adding markets and capabilities incrementally rather than relying on a single transformational acquisition. The approach is partly supported by the capital Nigerian banks have raised following the Central Bank of Nigeria’s recapitalisation exercise. Nigerian banks raised more than N4.65 trillion in fresh capital to meet new minimum capital requirements, giving some lenders additional capacity to pursue expansion at home and across the continent. Access Bank became the first lender to exceed its new capital threshold after raising N351 billion ($242 million) through a rights issue. Speaking during the group’s 2024 investor call, Roosevelt Ogbonna, group managing director of Access Bank, said the capital raise was designed to fund expansion rather than simply meet regulatory requirements. “We have consistently stated that our capital raise had nothing to do with the Central Bank’s directive requiring banks to raise their minimum capital,” Ogbonna said. “The capital was deployed immediately, and its impact is already visible.” A significant portion of the proceeds financed the acquisition of Standard Chartered’s subsidiaries in Angola, Sierra Leone, Tanzania and The Gambia, alongside National Bank of Kenya and a majority stake in Mauritius-based AfrAsia Bank. The acquisitions have helped strengthen Access’s position as one of Africa’s most geographically diversified banking groups. The expansion is already changing the group’s earnings profile. Nigeria’s contribution to Access Holdings’ pre-tax profit fell to 37 percent between January and September 2025, from 61 percent two years earlier, while African subsidiaries nearly doubled their contribution to 35 percent. The UK and other international businesses accounted for the remaining 28 percent. Zenith Bank is pursuing a similar internationalisation strategy. The bank, which recently completed a capital raise of more than N350 billion ($242 million), has set an ambitious target of generating about half of its profits outside Nigeria over the medium term. Related News IGP vows thorough probe into deaths of 37 suspected miners Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment South Africa bets bigger South Africa’s approach is more concentrated. Nedbank agreed to acquire about 66 percent of Kenya-based NCBA Group in a transaction valued at roughly $855 million-$856 million, making it the largest pure banking transaction covered in the report. Rather than building its East African presence through a series of smaller acquisitions, Nedbank is using one major transaction to gain immediate scale across multiple markets. The deal would give the South African lender an East African platform spanning Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, while combining Nedbank’s corporate and investment banking capabilities with NCBA’s digital and retail reach.

title: Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Africa > Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit Angola cuts rates to lowest since 2016 as inflation hits single digit Faith Omoboye September 18, 2026 Share ads Angola’s central bank has cut its key interest rate by 100 basis points to 14.75 percent, its third consecutive reduction, as inflation fell to single digits for the first time in more than a decade. The National Bank of Angola lowered its policy rate from 15.75 percent at its September 2026 meeting on Tuesday, taking the benchmark to its lowest level since 2016 as price pressures continued to ease and economic growth strengthened. Inflation fell to 8.78 percent year on year in August from 9.33 percent in July, extending a downward trend that began in mid 2024. It was the lowest inflation rate recorded in Angola since April 2015. The central bank maintained its year end inflation forecast at 8.6 percent, suggesting that policymakers expect price pressures to continue easing despite uncertainty created by the conflict in the Middle East. The latest rate cut follows a 125 basis point reduction in July and a 50 basis point cut in May, bringing the total reduction in the policy rate this year to 275 basis points. ads ads The central bank also raised its economic growth forecast for 2026 sharply to 6.15 percent from 3.6 percent previously, citing stronger performance in both the oil and non-oil sectors. Official data showed the economy expanded 8.74 percent year on year in the second quarter, up from 5.32 percent in the first quarter and marking its strongest growth since the second quarter of 2022. The improved outlook comes as Angola benefits from higher global energy prices, although policymakers remain alert to risks from the conflict in the Middle East and its impact on shipping, energy costs and imported goods. Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Manuel Tiago Dias, governor of the National Bank of Angola, said inflation was still expected to end the year at 8.6 percent. ads ads The easing inflation environment gives the central bank more room to reduce borrowing costs while supporting economic activity, although the pace of further cuts will depend on how prices, the exchange rate and external conditions develop. Liandra da Silva, an economist at Nedbank, told Reuters that Angola’s position as an oil exporter provided some protection against external shocks, but warned that higher shipping costs and imported input prices could still add to inflation. Angola’s stronger oil revenues have also drawn attention to how the government manages the additional income. The International Monetary Fund has urged the government to use oil revenue windfalls to reduce debt and build fiscal buffers rather than allowing higher oil earnings to translate into greater spending. Vera Daves de Sousa, Angola’s Finance Minister, told Reuters last week that the government was likely to raise its 2027 oil price assumption from the $61 per barrel used in this year’s budget, while maintaining a conservative approach to its forecasts. For the central bank, the combination of falling inflation and stronger economic growth provides a more favourable environment for monetary easing. However, external risks remain, particularly if higher energy prices and transport costs feed into imported inflation. title: NBC at 75: Seven decades of bottling, building and betting on Nigeria - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > NBC at 75: Seven decades of bottling, building and betting on Nigeria NBC at 75: Seven decades of bottling, building and betting on Nigeria Chinwe Michael September 17, 2026 Share ads Seventy-five years after it began production from a single factory in Ebute Metta, Lagos, Nigerian Bottling Company (NBC) Ltd has grown into one of Nigeria’s most established manufacturing businesses, building a nationwide footprint while deepening its links with local suppliers, workers, communities, and consumers. The company, a member of the Coca-Cola HBC Group, marked the milestone with a gala at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre in Abuja, bringing together government officials, business leaders, and stakeholders to celebrate its seven-decade presence in Nigeria. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, represented by George Akume, Secretary to the Government of the Federation, described NBC’s 75-year journey as an important milestone for Nigeria’s industrial development. “Seventy-five years ago, Nigerian Bottling Company began a journey in Lagos. Tonight, we celebrate what that journey has produced. But more importantly, we look forward to what the next chapter can bring: more investment, stronger industries, better jobs, deeper local production and greater opportunities for Nigerians,” Akume said. He said the government welcomed companies prepared to manufacture in Nigeria, develop local talent, strengthen domestic supply chains and invest in the communities where they operate. ads ads From Ebute Metta to a nationwide footprint NBC’s Nigerian story began in 1951 when it commenced production in Ebute Metta. Seventy-five years later, the company operates eight plants, 11 depots and 52 commercial territories across the country. Its growth has created an extensive network spanning manufacturing, logistics, distribution and retail, while connecting the company to local suppliers and agricultural value chains. An economic impact study by Steward Redqueen found that the wider Coca-Cola system contributed approximately $1 billion in value-added economic activity across its Nigerian value chain in 2024. The system supported more than 160,000 jobs during the year, including nearly 3,000 direct positions and about 157,200 jobs across retail, agriculture, manufacturing, transport, services, and other sectors. ads ads The study also estimated that the Coca-Cola system sourced almost $601 million worth of goods and services from Nigerian suppliers in 2024. For NBC, the figures underscore how a manufacturing operation established 75 years ago has developed into a broader economic ecosystem. Anastassis G. David, chairman of Coca-Cola HBC, said Anastasios Leventis’s 1951 decision to secure Coca-Cola rights across Nigeria represented a long-term bet on the country. “In 1951, Anastasios Leventis negotiated the rights for the whole of Nigeria. It was a big, bold decision, but it was also a statement of belief,” David said. He said the decision reflected confidence in Nigeria’s importance, scale and prospects, as well as in the potential of its people and communities. “That belief echoes our own confidence in Nigeria’s future, which remains as strong today as it has ever been,” he said. Built on consistency and trust Sola David-Borha, chairperson of the NBC board, said the company’s ability to remain relevant over seven and a half decades had been built on trust, consistency and sound governance. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 Goran Sladic, managing director of NBC, described the company’s history as inseparable from Nigeria’s economic and social development. “Seventy-five years of Nigerian Bottling Company is 75 years of growing with Nigeria. We are proud of the role we have played in creating opportunities, developing people, supporting communities, and strengthening local value chains,” Sladic said. “As we look to the future, our ambition is to build on that legacy and continue creating value for years to come.” The anniversary comes as the company and its parent group seek to extend that legacy through further investments in local manufacturing. Betting on the next 75 years Zoran Bogdanovic, chief executive officer of Coca-Cola HBC, reaffirmed the group’s commitment to Nigeria, saying the anniversary represented more than longevity. “This is a remarkable milestone for any company. For us, it represents far more than longevity. It reflects a shared history with Nigeria, a country where Coca-Cola HBC’s story began, and a history of which we are very proud,” he said. Coca-Cola HBC has committed to invest up to $1 billion in Nigeria over five years, subject to a predictable and enabling business environment. Bogdanovic said the group had already begun advancing the commitment through investments aimed at expanding manufacturing capacity at NBC’s Asejire plant in Oyo State and Challawa plant in Kano State. The investments are expected to increase production capacity while strengthening opportunities across the local manufacturing and supply ecosystem. Beyond its manufacturing operations, Coca-Cola HBC is also directing capital towards entrepreneurship and social development. The Coca-Cola HBC Foundation announced a $1.25 million commitment over three years to support young Nigerian entrepreneurs in the hospitality and food-service sector. The initiative will provide business grants, entrepreneurship training, business formalisation support and mentorship. title: Oando gets shareholders approval for cross-border listings - Businessday NG

Share ads A favourable resolution was given by shareholders at the 47th Annual General Meeting (AGM) of Oando Plc authorising the directors to effect the listing of the Company’s shares on other stock exchange(s) as they may deem fit (including cross-border listings). title: From private scale to public markets: What Johannesburg revealed about Africa’s next generation of tech companies - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Markets > From private scale to public markets: What Johannesburg revealed about Africa’s next generation of tech companies From private scale to public markets: What Johannesburg revealed about Africa’s next generation of tech companies Iheanyi Nwachukwu September 14, 2026 Share ads Nearly two months after the AT50 Index convened its first African Exchange Activation at the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), one question from the discussions remains unresolved: Africa has built technology companies of significant private-market scale, but is the market infrastructure around them developing quickly enough to connect that scale with long-term institutional capital? Africa’s technology ecosystem has changed considerably over the past decade. Companies that were once discussed primarily through the language of venture capital, startup formation and fundraising are increasingly operating across multiple countries, generating significant revenues, employing thousands of people and building increasingly complex financial and operational infrastructure. But as companies mature, the capital they require changes too. That transition was at the centre of discussions on July 15, when the AT50 Index held its first African Exchange Activation at the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, following the benchmark’s global launch at the London Stock Exchange in January. The gathering brought together the JSE, African banks, institutional investors, policymakers, professional advisers and executives from some of the continent’s largest private technology companies. ads ads Nearly two months later, the most important question raised in Johannesburg was not whether every African technology company should pursue a public listing. It was whether Africa has built enough of the infrastructure required to give companies credible choices as they move beyond traditional venture funding. Scale changes the capital conversation … Sam Mokorosi, Head of Origination and Deals at the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, described the transition in straightforward terms. “As companies reach this level of scale, the conversation naturally begins to evolve,” Mokorosi said at the activation. “The focus shifts from simply building businesses to sustaining long-term growth, and increasingly from raising capital to accessing the right kind of capital.” That distinction matters. The financing requirements of an early-stage company are fundamentally different from those of a business operating across several markets, handling significant transaction volumes and contemplating acquisitions, secondary liquidity or eventual public-market participation. ads ads The JSE has been working to broaden those pathways, including simplifying aspects of the listing process while retaining governance standards and developing routes to capital through secondary listings and private placements. “Growth does not follow a single path, and neither does capital formation,” Mokorosi said. “We believe that efficient access to capital and strong corporate governance should go hand in hand.” That was echoed by Standard Bank Corporate & Investment Banking, the Lead Banking Partner for the AT50 African Exchange Activation programme. Richard Stout, Head of Equity Capital Markets at Standard Bank CIB, described the initiative following Johannesburg as supporting the pathway “from private capital to public markets” and highlighted the importance of collaboration between founders, investors, exchanges and banking partners as companies prepare to scale and access public markets. The significance is not simply whether an IPO happens. The deeper issue is whether a functioning institutional ecosystem exists around companies before they reach that point. Institutional capital requires more than growth For much of Africa’s recent technology cycle, rapid growth and successive fundraising rounds provided some of the most visible signals of company progress. Institutional investors assess businesses differently. Governance, disclosure, financial controls, predictable reporting, management depth and the ability to compare performance against peers become increasingly important alongside revenue growth. That point emerged repeatedly in Johannesburg. Khusela Sangoni Diko, Chairperson of South Africa’s Parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Communications and Digital Technologies, put it succinctly: “Strong governance is far more than a compliance exercise. It is a competitive advantage.” Her participation was significant because it connected what can appear to be a specialist capital-markets debate with a wider question about South Africa’s digital economy. Parliament itself framed the Johannesburg discussion around how innovation, investment and capital formation could accelerate the country’s digital economy and contribute to inclusive growth. Technology executives reinforced the same point from inside the companies themselves. Carsten Höltkemeyer, CEO of South African fintech Yoco, argued that scaling a technology business increasingly requires “the operational maturity expected by larger, long-term investors.” Related News Two-thirds of Africans oppose more foreign job seekers, refugees – Report AFRICA FINANCE IN BRIEF:Private capital surges as African markets deepen cross border investment Ivory Coast targets 2027 gold refinery start as it seeks top producer spot Fidelis Chiwara, Flutterwave’s Head of Global Expansion described the practical tension companies face between continuing to pursue growth opportunities and investing in compliance, systems and operational resilience. title: Afreximbank, ZEP-RE move to close skills gap threatening Africa’s cross-border trade - Businessday NG
text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Companies > Afreximbank, ZEP-RE move to close skills gap threatening Africa’s cross-border trade Afreximbank, ZEP-RE move to close skills gap threatening Africa’s cross-border trade Hope Moses-Ashike September 17, 2026 Share ads The African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and ZEP-RE (PTA Reinsurance Company) have signed a three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen professional and institutional capacity in trade, insurance, reinsurance, risk management and trade facilitation across Africa. The partnership is aimed at addressing the skills and institutional capacity needed to support Africa’s expanding trade and investment ecosystem, particularly as cross-border transactions become increasingly complex. Under the agreement, Afreximbank Academy (AFRACAD) and ZEP-RE Academy will jointly develop and scale learning, research and knowledge programmes that combine Afreximbank’s expertise in African trade and trade finance with ZEP-RE’s experience in insurance, reinsurance and risk management. The MoU was signed at ZEP-RE’s offices in Nairobi by Stephen Tio Kauma, Group managing director, Human Resources, Afreximbank, and Jephita Gwatipedza, Group deputy chief executive officer and chief operating officer, ZEP-RE. Kauma said Africa’s ability to expand trade and investment depends not only on financial resources and infrastructure but also on knowledge, skills and institutional capacity across its markets. ads ads “Africa’s ability to expand trade and investment depends on more than financial resources and infrastructure. It also depends on knowledge, skills and institutional capacity across our markets,” he said. He said the partnership would combine complementary expertise in trade finance, insurance, reinsurance and risk management to develop practical and scalable learning and knowledge solutions for professionals and institutions across Africa. Gwatipedza said sustainable expansion of trade would require institutions that finance and facilitate commerce to understand, price and manage the risks involved. “Trade cannot expand sustainably unless the institutions that finance and facilitate it can also understand, price and manage the risks involved,” he said. ads ads He said the partnership would connect trade finance with insurance and reinsurance expertise and help strengthen institutional capability across African markets. Under the three-year partnership, AFRACAD and ZEP-RE Academy will collaborate across three strategic areas, beginning with the co-creation of digital learning content, including e-learning courses, toolkits and African case studies. Related News Netflix Reviews: Why Did I Get Married The importance of consistent branding across all platforms Top 10 sectors attracting global investment in 2026 Through a joint “content factory” approach, the institutions will identify thematic priorities and develop structured and reusable learning resources. The materials will be made available through AFRACAD’s digital learning platform and/or ZEP-RE Academy’s Learning Management System. The two institutions will also jointly design and deliver professional and executive development programmes covering areas such as risk and reinsurance, trade guarantees, trade facilitation, financial infrastructure and market development. The programmes may include short courses, executive masterclasses, certification programmes and other structured learning delivered physically, virtually or through blended formats. The partnership will also support research, knowledge creation and thought leadership through joint studies, webinars, policy dialogues and industry forums involving practitioners, regulators, development partners and private-sector leaders. The MoU builds on an existing partnership between Afreximbank and ZEP-RE. In 2025, the two institutions launched the Trans-Africa Bond Alliance (TABA) to strengthen insurance capacity, facilitate cross-border trade and support the movement of goods and investment across Africa. Since beginning operations in June 2025, TABA has supported approximately US$185 million in bonds in 2025 and US$280 million in the first quarter of 2026, with risks originating from 24 cedents across five countries. TABA supports Afreximbank’s African Collaborative Transit Guarantee Scheme (AACTGS) and the wider AfCFTA trade facilitation agenda by promoting a harmonised, technology-enabled approach to transit guarantees across African borders. The wider African Collaborative Transit Guarantee Scheme is supported by US$1 billion in guarantee limits, including a US$300 million facility being implemented with ZEP-RE in the COMESA region. The initiative aims to reduce reliance on multiple national transit bonds, release working capital otherwise tied up as collateral and improve the efficiency and predictability of cross-border trade. The latest MoU extends the collaboration into capacity building, with the two institutions seeking to strengthen the technical expertise and institutional knowledge required for increasingly sophisticated trade, insurance and risk solutions across African markets. The partnership is expected to build a stronger pool of African expertise capable of addressing issues at the intersection of trade, finance, insurance and risk, while supporting deeper regional integration and sustainable economic development across the continent. The MoU will initially run for three years and may be renewed by mutual agreement. text: Saturday, September 19, 2026 X BusinessDay Home Tax Calculator Companies Markets Economy Real Estate Agriculture Aviation Banking Transportation Maritime Legal Business Research post Sports BDFX BD Conferences BD Foundation BusinessDay Intelligence Adverts & Rates About US Our Board Our Management Our Profile Corporate Subscription Home > Markets > Investors inject billions of naira in first hour as Dangote Refinery IPO opens Investors inject billions of naira in first hour as Dangote Refinery IPO opens Pelumi Adesanya September 14, 2026 Share ads The Nigerian Exchange (NGX) witnessed an unprecedented flurry of activity on Monday morning as trading opened for the highly anticipated Dangote Refinery Initial Public Offering (IPO). Within the first hour of listing, billions of naira poured into the market, signaling immense institutional and retail demand for the historical capital raise. Speaking at the ‘Facts Behind the Offer’ presentation and ceremonial Gong Striking ceremony at the NGX headquarters in Lagos, Group President Aliko Dangote emphasised that the primary objective of the public offer is to broaden market access across the continent. “The primary purpose of this offer is to democratise the NGX,” Dangote stated during his address to market operators and banking executives. Read also: Dangote IPO crashes top investment apps as retail investors face downtime ads ads “It’s not about making money, as we have raised more than what we need as a group. The IPO is mostly about making sure the public enjoys part of this benefit as this is going to be the largest company in Africa.” The offering, which involves 4.1 billion ordinary shares, marks a key milestone in a journey that began 13 years ago in September 2013 when initial capital raising commenced. title: NGINX Open Source Governance
text: Join us for the first quarterly NGINX Community Call on July 22nd to connect and discuss NGINX development. NGINX Open Source Governance Open source changed the world. NGINX is proud to be part of that change, from our very beginning. NGINX embraces open source ethos and intends to remain an active contributor and leader in the ecosystem. This is encapsulated by our Core Commitments and Principles, which serve to help the longevity, transparency, and impact of our open source projects. Our Core Commitments We will be open, consistent, transparent, and fair in our acceptance of contributions. We will continue to enhance existing active projects. We will release new projects that move technology forward. We will continue to offer projects under OSI-approved software licenses. We will not remove and commercialize existing projects or features. We will not impose limits on the use of our projects. NGINX Open Source Principles All contributions are reviewed by the technical committee for that project. Our contribution review discussions are available and publicly viewable to provide transparency. Project roadmaps are public and future direction is discussed in the open.

title: F5 Acquires NGINX to Bridge NetOps & DevOps, Providing Customers with Consistent Application Services Across Every Environment | F5
text: Stay current to protect your environment with F5 Hardened Releases. Learn more F5 Acquires NGINX to Bridge NetOps & DevOps, Providing Customers with Consistent Application Services Across Every Environment Published March 11, 2019 Contacts Nathan Misner Sr. Director of Global Communications F5 (206) 272-7494 n.misner@F5.com Suzanne DuLong VP, Investor Relations F5 (206) 272-7049 s.dulong@f5.com Jesica Church Marketing NGINX, Inc. (415) 706-1804 NGINX@pancomm.com F5, the global leader in multi-cloud application services, announces the acquisition of NGINX, an open source leader in application delivery. Strategic acquisition and organic investment to secure long-term revenue and EPS growth. Together, F5 and NGINX will enable multi-cloud application services across all environments, providing the ease-of-use and flexibility developers require while also delivering the scale, security, reliability and enterprise readiness network operations teams demand. F5 is committed to continued innovation and increasing investment in the NGINX open source project to empower NGINX’s widespread user communities. F5 will maintain the brand with current NGINX CEO, Gus Robertson, and founders, Igor Sysoev and Maxim Konovalov, joining F5 to continue to lead NGINX. SEATTLE and SAN FRANCISCO – F5 Networks , Inc. (NASDAQ: FFIV ) and NGINX today announced a definitive agreement under which F5 will acquire all issued and outstanding shares of privately held NGINX for a total enterprise value of approximately $670 million, subject to certain adjustments. “F5’s acquisition of NGINX strengthens our growth trajectory by accelerating our software and multi-cloud transformation,” said François Locoh-Donou, President & CEO of F5. “By bringing F5’s world-class application security and rich application services portfolio for improving performance, availability, and management together with NGINX’s leading software application delivery and API management solutions, unparalleled credibility and brand recognition in the DevOps community, and massive open source user base, we bridge the divide between NetOps and DevOps with consistent application services across an enterprise’s multi-cloud environment.” “We believe every organization can benefit from the agility and flexibility enabled by modern technologies without compromising on security, manageability, and reliability,” continued Locoh-Donou. “The combined company will enable every customer—from the app developer to the network engineer to the security specialist—with the tools they need to ensure their apps are available and secure across every platform, from the enterprise data center to private and public clouds.” F5 will enhance NGINX’s current offerings with F5 security solutions and will integrate F5 cloud-native innovations with NGINX’s software load balancing technology, accelerating F5’s time to market of application services for modern, containerized applications. F5 will also leverage its global sales force, channel infrastructure, and partner ecosystem to scale NGINX selling opportunities to the enterprise. “NGINX and F5 share the same mission and vision. We both believe applications are at the heart of driving digital transformation. And we both believe that an end-to-end application infrastructure—one that spans from code to customer—is needed to deliver apps across a multi-cloud environment,” said Gus Robertson, CEO of NGINX, Inc. “I’m excited to continue this journey by adding the power of NGINX’s open source innovation to F5’s ADC leadership and enterprise reach. F5 gains depth with solutions designed for DevOps, while NGINX gains breadth with access to tens of thousands of customers and partners.” NGINX’s thriving open source community was one of the most attractive elements of this combination, and F5 recognizes the trust that the user community has in NGINX’s technology. Open source is a core part of F5’s multi-cloud strategy and a driver for F5’s next phase of innovation. As such, F5 is committed to continued innovation and increasing investment in the NGINX open source project to empower NGINX’s widespread user communities. F5 expects the combination with NGINX will accelerate its product integrations with leading open source projects and will enhance its strong technology partnerships with open source vendors. Upon closing of the acquisition, F5 will maintain the NGINX brand. Gus Robertson, along with NGINX founders Igor Sysoev and Maxim Konovalov, will join F5 and will continue to lead NGINX. Robertson will join F5’s senior management team, reporting to François Locoh-Donou. F5 will maintain NGINX’s operations in San Francisco, California and other locations globally. Transaction Details The acquisition of NGINX is expected to increase F5’s software revenue growth and increase the Company’s software revenue mix in fiscal year 2019. It secures F5’s Horizon 2 (fiscal year 2021 to fiscal year 2022) objectives of mid-to-high single-digit revenue and double-digit non-GAAP earnings per share growth. Short-term, the Company expects that the acquisition and organic investment in new and emerging solutions will result in modest earnings dilution in fiscal years 2019 and 2020.
